steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine Translation (MT) has historically been under two influences that seem at first glance (prima facie) to contradict each other. One of the goals of MT research is to give means to convert sentences from any language into any other language. On the one hand, the generalization capabilities depend on our systems producing representations that are language agnostic. On the other hand, MT models should be good at encoding the specifics of the source languages. The first of these trends has deeply marked the field, and the concept of an 'interlingua' runs through most of the history of MT research, from early work to more recent work. The second trend has recently motivated the development of modular approaches, where the network parameters are tied specifically to a specific language.

So how can these two trends, which seem paradoxical, be reconciled? One approach that looks promising is to include fully-shared subnetworks in modular architectures, and especially bridge components. It has been argued that they foster language-independent representations and also zero-shot generalization capabilities. Our aim is to carefully assess whether modular architectures in general, and bridges, really do foster greater generalization capabilities.

- Study and findings
  - six architectures, five of them modular
  - focus on generalization: unseen translation directions + novel domains
  - modular systems still struggle to stay competitive with fully-shared MT systems when not all translation directions available
  - affects systems with and without fixed-size bridges equally
  - encoder-sharing modular designs can rival/outperform non-modular in a wide range of scenarios
  - all other systems struggle in zero-shot and out-of-distribution conditions
  - -> strongly questions that fully-shared sub-networks in modular MT improve generalization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine Translation (MT) has historically been under two influences that seem at first glance (prima facie) to contradict each other. One of the goals of MT research is to give means to convert sentences from any language into any other language. On the one hand, the generalization capabilities depend on our systems producing representations that are language agnostic. On the other hand, MT models should be good at encoding the specifics of the source languages. The first of these trends has deeply marked the field, and the concept of an 'interlingua' runs through most of the history of MT research, from early work to more recent work. The second trend has recently motivated the development of modular approaches, where the network parameters are tied specifically to a specific language.

So how can these two trends, which seem paradoxical, be reconciled? One approach that looks promising is to include fully-shared subnetworks in modular architectures, and especially bridge components. It has been argued that they foster language-independent representations and also zero-shot generalization capabilities. Our aim is to carefully assess whether modular architectures in general, and bridges, really do foster greater generalization capabilities.

To do this we study six architectures, and five of them are modular. We focus in particular on how they generalize, both to translation directions that were not seen and to novel domains. We find that modular systems still struggle to stay competitive with fully-shared MT systems in scenarios where not all translation directions are available, and this conclusion affects systems with and without fixed-size bridges equally. Encoder-sharing modular designs can rival or outperform non-modular settings in a wide range of scenarios, but all the other systems we study struggle in zero-shot and out-of-distribution conditions. This strongly questions the idea that fully-shared sub-networks in modular MT systems can improve their generalization capabilities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine Translation (MT) has historically been under two influences that seem prima facie contradictory. One of the goals of MT research is to provide means of converting sentences from any language to any other. On the one hand, generalization capabilities depend on our systems producing language agnostic representations. On the other hand, MT models should be apt at encoding the specifics of source languages [1]. The former trend has deeply marked this field: the concept of an ‘interlingua’ runs through most of the history of MT research, from [2] to [3]. The latter has recently motivated the development of modular approaches, where network parameters are tied to a specific language.

How can we reconcile these two seemingly paradoxical trends? One promising approach is to include fully-shared subnetworks in modular architectures, and especially bridge components, which have been argued to foster language-independent representations [4] as well as zero-shot generalization capabilities [5]. Our aim is to carefully assess whether modular architectures in general, and bridges in particular, do indeed foster greater generalization capabilities.

We therefore study six architectures, five of which are modular, focusing in particular on how they generalize, both to unseen translation directions and to novel domains. We find that modular systems still struggle to remain competitive with fully-shared MT systems in scenarios where not all translation directions are available, a conclusion that affects systems with and without fixed-size bridges equally. While encoder-sharing modular designs can rival or outperform non-modular settings in a wide range of scenarios, all other systems we study struggle in zero-shot and out-of-distribution conditions, which strongly questions whether fully-shared sub-networks in modular MT systems can improve their generalization capabilities.

References:
[1] Belinkov et al. (2017) Yonatan Belinkov, Nadir Durrani, Fahim Dalvi, Hassan Sajjad, and James Glass. 2017. What do neural machine translation models learn about morphology?
